# Assessment and Classification of Obesity

The accurate assessment of obesity is a prerequisite for appropriate clinical decision-making, yet the tools available to clinicians vary substantially in their complexity, accessibility, and validity. Body mass index (BMI), calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres, remains the most widely used metric for population-level and clinical classification of adiposity. The World Health Organization categorises BMI into underweight (below 18.5 kg/m²), normal weight (18.5–24.9 kg/m²), overweight (25.0–29.9 kg/m²), and obesity (30.0 kg/m² and above), with obesity further subdivided into class I (30.0–34.9 kg/m²), class II (35.0–39.9 kg/m²), and class III, or severe obesity (40.0 kg/m² and above). These thresholds underpin treatment eligibility criteria across pharmacological, endoscopic, and surgical domains and are enshrined in clinical practice guidelines internationally [@Garvey2016American]. Recognising that Asian populations accrue cardiometabolic risk at lower thresholds of adiposity, the WHO Expert Consultation proposed revised Asia-Pacific cut-points: overweight at a BMI of 23.0 kg/m² or above and obesity at 27.5 kg/m² or above. These ethnicity-specific thresholds are now integrated into guidelines across East and South Asia and are increasingly advocated in multiethnic Western clinical settings to avoid systematic underdiagnosis in these populations [@WilsonPetruk2023Obesity].

Despite its administrative convenience, BMI is an imprecise surrogate for adiposity that carries several well-characterised limitations. Because BMI is derived from total body mass relative to height, it cannot distinguish fat mass from lean mass; muscular individuals and those with sarcopenia may therefore be misclassified. Equally important, BMI provides no information about the anatomical distribution of adipose tissue, a distinction of considerable physiological consequence. Two individuals with identical BMI values may differ dramatically in cardiometabolic risk depending on the relative proportions of visceral and subcutaneous fat. The mortality data are also more nuanced than the WHO classification suggests: the landmark meta-analysis by @Flegal2013Association, pooling data from 97 prospective studies and more than 2.88 million individuals, found that grade 1 obesity (BMI 30.0–34.9 kg/m²) was not associated with significantly increased all-cause mortality compared with normal weight, whereas grades II and III combined were associated with a hazard ratio of 1.29 (95% CI 1.18–1.41). This finding, while contested methodologically, underscores that BMI alone is insufficient to stratify individual risk [@Flegal2013Association].

The limitations of BMI have stimulated interest in measures that better capture the distribution and health consequences of adiposity. Waist circumference is the most clinically practical of these measures. The National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP-ATP III) defines abdominal obesity as waist circumference exceeding 102 cm in men and 88 cm in women, thresholds associated with substantially elevated risk of metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease. As with BMI, ethnicity-specific thresholds are recognised: the International Diabetes Federation uses 90 cm in Asian men and 80 cm in Asian women. The waist-to-height ratio — ideally maintained below 0.5 across adulthood — combines information about central fat distribution with an implicit adjustment for stature and has demonstrated predictive validity for cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes across diverse populations [@Ryan2018Guideline]. Where greater precision is required, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) serves as the clinical gold standard for body composition assessment, enabling direct quantification of fat mass, lean mass, and visceral adipose tissue, and is particularly valuable in the assessment of sarcopenic obesity and in the evaluation of treatment response in clinical trials.

The Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS), proposed by @Sharma2009Proposed, represents a substantive advance beyond purely anthropometric classification by incorporating the functional and clinical consequences of obesity. The EOSS assigns patients to one of five stages based on the presence and severity of metabolic, physical, and mental health complications. Stage 0 denotes no apparent risk factors, functional limitations, or psychological symptoms despite excess adiposity; stage 1 indicates subclinical risk factors such as borderline hypertension or fasting glucose impairment; stage 2 encompasses established comorbidities including type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea, or moderate functional limitations; stage 3 characterises severe organ damage, significant disability, or major psychiatric illness; and stage 4 reflects end-stage organ failure or extreme functional incapacity. The clinical utility of this staging scheme is that it shifts the treatment imperative away from BMI alone and toward the burden of obesity-related illness. Importantly, epidemiological analyses have demonstrated that EOSS predicts all-cause mortality independently of and more accurately than BMI, challenging the notion that weight reduction should be pursued uniformly across all individuals with elevated BMI [@Sharma2009Proposed; @Garvey2016American].

Building on similar principles, the Adiposity-Based Chronic Disease (ABCD) framework was proposed as a diagnostic and staging framework that emphasises complications as the primary driver of clinical action. Within the ABCD construct, abnormal adiposity constitutes the primary diagnosis, while the nature and severity of metabolic (such as dysglycaemia, dyslipidaemia, and hypertension), biomechanical (such as osteoarthritis and sleep-disordered breathing), and psychological (such as depression and binge eating disorder) complications determine staging and guide treatment intensity. The explicit complications-driven orientation of the ABCD framework represents a movement away from weight-centric medicine toward a model in which cardiometabolic and functional health outcomes, rather than weight per se, anchor the therapeutic rationale [@Garvey2016American].

A comprehensive metabolic risk assessment is therefore integral to the obesity evaluation. Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed according to either the IDF or NCEP-ATP III criteria when three or more of the following are present: elevated waist circumference (using ethnicity-appropriate thresholds), fasting plasma glucose at or above 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) or established type 2 diabetes, serum triglycerides at or above 1.7 mmol/L (150 mg/dL), HDL-cholesterol below 1.0 mmol/L (40 mg/dL) in men or below 1.3 mmol/L (50 mg/dL) in women, and blood pressure at or above 130/85 mmHg or pharmacological treatment for hypertension. Beyond these components, the clinical assessment of obesity should incorporate HbA1c and fasting glucose for glycaemic stratification, a full fasting lipid profile, and a cardiovascular risk calculator such as the Pooled Cohort Equations or SCORE2, which integrate multiple risk factors into absolute 10-year cardiovascular event probabilities [@Apovian2015Pharmacological]. Given the high prevalence of metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease in this population, hepatic evaluation using non-invasive indices such as the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) score and liver stiffness measurement by elastography is increasingly recommended as part of the initial workup.

Assessment must also account for clinically important variations in the obesity phenotype that standard metrics fail to capture. Sarcopenic obesity — defined by the coexistence of excess adiposity and reduced muscle mass or strength — is increasingly prevalent in older adults and confers risks not adequately reflected in BMI-based classifications; it is best identified through DXA-based body composition measurement combined with grip strength or functional performance testing. Conversely, so-called normal-weight metabolic obesity describes individuals whose BMI falls within the normal range yet who harbour excess visceral adiposity and a markedly adverse cardiometabolic risk profile, further illustrating the limitations of weight-based assessment. The obesity paradox — observed associations between overweight or grade 1 obesity and improved survival in certain chronic diseases including heart failure and chronic kidney disease — complicates treatment decisions in these populations and may reflect, at least in part, methodological confounding by reverse causation and BMI's insensitivity to body composition. Finally, weight assessment in pregnancy requires specific consideration: gestational weight gain recommendations from the Institute of Medicine are stratified by pre-pregnancy BMI and reflect the dual imperative of supporting fetal development while minimising the risk of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, and excessive postpartum weight retention. Taken together, these considerations affirm that a clinically meaningful assessment of obesity must integrate anthropometric measurements, body composition data, the full cardiometabolic risk profile, and the broader functional and psychological context of the individual patient.
